title: Volcanoes That Made History - Nautilus
gist: A history piece recounts how the 1883 Krakatau eruption obliterated islands between Java and Sumatra, killed more than 36,000 people mostly via tsunamis, and became known worldwide within days—illustrating how enormous eruptions reshaped Earth's climate and societies.

insights.claim: On the morning of August 27, 1883, a volcanic eruption obliterated two islands in the strait between Java and Sumatra and most of a third.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Witze
insights.so_what: Anchors the scale of one of history's most consequential volcanic disasters.
insights.locator: On the morning of August 27, 1883, a volcanic eruption had obliterated two islands

insights.claim: More than 36,000 people perished in the Krakatau eruption, the majority in devastating tsunamis radiating from the explosion.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Witze
insights.so_what: Quantifies the human toll and identifies tsunamis, not the blast, as the main killer.

themes.theme: Global reach and legacy of eruptions

insights.claim: News of the Krakatau disaster spread worldwide within days via telegram, with early wires reporting detonations, falling stones, and villages washed away.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Witze
insights.so_what: Illustrates how 19th-century communications technology turned a local catastrophe into a global event.
insights.quote: Where once Mount Krakatau stood the sea now plays.
insights.locator: The first telegram arrived in Singapore

insights.claim: Long after their lava stopped flowing, enormous volcanic eruptions altered Earth's climate and societies across the globe.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Witze
insights.so_what: Frames volcanic eruptions as long-tail drivers of climatic and social change, not just immediate disasters.
insights.locator: enormous eruptions altered Earth’s climate and societies all over the globe
